 Perseverance Finds Mars Dust Fine Enough to Reach Astronaut Lungs and Brain
 Spacesuit fabric sorts Mars dust by size class: Teflon traps 100-nm ultrafines, Vectran coarser fraction
 By 
 James Whitaker 
 Published: Oct 27 2026, 11:32 PM EDT 
 Share on Facebook

 This 360-degree panorama from NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover shows Neretva Vallis, the dusty, long-dried river channel that cuts through the western rim of Mars’ Jezero Crater. 
 Nasa.gov 
 For the first time in the history of planetary exploration, scientists have directly measured Mars dust particle sizes on the Martian surface — and confirmed that a significant fraction fall below the 2.5-micrometer (µm) threshold at which particles penetrate deep into human lungs, with some reaching the 100-nanometer (nm) threshold at which particles can travel via the olfactory nerve directly to the brain.
 A study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) by Scott VanBommel of Washington University in St. Louis and colleagues reports the first direct in-situ evidence of both fine (PM2.5, ≤2.5 µm) and ultrafine (PM0.1, ≤100 nm) Martian dust particles — confirming two of the most medically significant size thresholds are present in the dust astronauts will inevitably encounter during future crewed missions. The finding carries an immediate engineering implication that the data surfaces but that existing mission planning has not yet fully absorbed: different spacesuit fabrics attract different particle size classes through electrostatic charging, meaning the choice of suit material determines which hazard fraction astronauts concentrate on their suits and carry into pressurized habitats.
 How Perseverance Measured What No Mission Has Measured Before
 The finding emerged from an unlikely source: a quality-control plate. PIXL — the Planetary Instrument for X-ray Lithochemistry on Perseverance's robotic arm — uses a flat calibration target of Teflon (PTFE) and polished basaltic glass to verify its X-ray fluorescence (XRF) performance each day. The target was designed to confirm the instrument was producing accurate elemental maps of Mars rocks. But over 1,645 Martian sols of operation in Jezero Crater, it also silently collected whatever dust settled onto it from the Martian atmosphere.
 PIXL works by focusing a micro-scale X-ray beam onto a target surface, exciting the atoms in that material to emit characteristic fluorescent X-rays. By scanning the beam across a surface and measuring which X-ray energies come back at each position, PIXL produces a high-resolution elemental map — a square-by-square picture of what each patch of surface is made of. VanBommel's team turned this capability on the accumulated dust. By cross-referencing PIXL's elemental fluorescence maps with optical images from SHERLOC's WATSON camera, researchers could locate individual dust particles and infer their sizes from the spatial footprint of each fluorescence signal. Particles in the 100 nm to 2.5 µm range were distinguishable because PIXL's micro-focus beam is sensitive enough to detect sub-pixel-scale emission differences between a clean surface and a particle-covered one.
 The team also used a second trapping surface as a cross-check: SHERLOC carries 10 small actual spacesuit material swatches — each 20mm × 20mm (0.79 × 0.79 in) — including Teflon and Vectran, an aromatic polyester-polyamide fiber used in suit construction, as part of an experiment to assess how Martian conditions affect materials used on astronaut suits. Those swatches had also been collecting dust across the entire mission. Together, the calibration plate and the spacesuit swatches gave researchers a paired comparison: the same Martian dust supply, captured on two different material types, over the same 1,645-sol period.
 Why Fabric Choice Determines Which Particles Enter Your Helmet
 The comparison revealed something the research team had not anticipated. Teflon and Vectran did not simply collect the same mixture of particles — they sorted them by size.
 The mechanism is electrostatic. In the dry, low-humidity environment of Mars, dust grains acquire electric charge through triboelectric collisions — grain-on-grain impacts during dust storms and dust devils, where different materials exchange electrons depending on their surface properties. Different materials carry different surface potentials, which determines which size class of charged grain they attract most strongly. Because ultrafine particles have extremely high surface-to-mass ratios, even modest electrostatic forces can dominate over gravity, making them more susceptible to capture by one material than another. Teflon, with its strongly negative triboelectric charge, concentrated smaller and ultrafine particles — reaching down into the sub-100 nm range. Vectran, with a different surface potential, attracted preferentially larger particles within the fine-particle spectrum, averaging around 2 µm.
 This finding surfaces a specific implication for suit design that existing mission-planning frameworks have not yet addressed: selecting a Teflon-dominant suit fabric concentrates the most medically dangerous particle fraction — ultrafine, brain-transport-threshold particles — on the outer surface of the suit. When an astronaut enters a habitat and removes that suit, they potentially introduce proportionally more ultrafine particles into the crew's breathing environment than a Vectran-dominant suit would. The choice of suit material is not only a durability and thermal management decision; it is a particle-size-sorting decision with consequences for airborne exposure indoors.
 What These Particles Do in a Human Body
 The medical significance of the two thresholds VanBommel's team confirmed follows from decades of Earth-based air quality research. Fine particulate matter — particles with aerodynamic diameters at or below 2.5 µm — can travel past the bronchioles into the alveolar sacs, where gas exchange occurs between the lungs and the bloodstream. At that depth, particles can cross the air-blood barrier and enter circulation, reaching the heart, kidneys, and brain. The EPA's 24-hour standard for PM2.5 stands at 35 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m³) for outdoor air; no occupational standard yet exists for the specific chemistry of Martian dust.
 Ultrafine particles — below 100 nm — take an additional route. Their small size allows them to travel along olfactory nerve fiber bundles, bypassing the blood-brain barrier entirely and depositing in the brain. Research has linked ultrafine particle exposure to neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration; no established occupational exposure standard addresses this olfactory-nerve pathway specifically.
 Martian dust compounds these inhalation risks with chemistry. Independent analysis has found that Martian regolith contains perchlorates — the ClO₄⁻ ion — at concentrations of roughly 0.5 to 1 percent by weight, 100 to 1,000 times higher than typical Earth soil. Perchlorate is a potent competitive inhibitor of the sodium-iodide symporter in the thyroid gland — it blocks iodide uptake, reducing production of thyroid hormones T3 and T4. The EPA's oral reference dose for perchlorate is 0.0007 milligrams per kilogram of body weight per day; for an astronaut inhaling fine-particle perchlorate in a confined habitat, cumulative thyroid exposure over months represents a documented physiological risk with no established mitigation beyond preventing inhalation in the first place.
 Mars dust also carries reactive nanophase iron oxides — iron particles so small that their surface chemistry differs from bulk iron oxide, generating reactive oxygen species on contact with lung tissue. A 2025 study in GeoHealth by Justin Wang, Brian Hynek, and colleagues at the University of Colorado Boulder and USC analyzed Martian dust composition from rover data and meteorite samples, identifying perchlorates, silicates, iron oxides, arsenic, and beryllium — and estimating an average grain size of roughly 3 µm, confirming that a substantial fraction already falls below PM10 threshold.
 CU Boulder geologist Brian Hynek said at the time of the 2025 findings: "We really need to characterize this dust so that we know what the hazards are." VanBommel's 2026 PNAS study now provides the first direct particle size measurements from the Martian surface itself, replacing distribution estimates with in-situ confirmation.
 Silicosis Research Frames the Risk Astronauts Face
 The medical framework for respirable mineral dust comes from occupational medicine. Silicosis — lung fibrosis caused by inhaled crystalline silica particles smaller than 10 µm — has killed tens of thousands of workers across mining, construction, and manufacturing industries. The mechanism: alveolar macrophages engulf silica particles, fail to clear them, and release inflammatory mediators (TNF-α, IL-1β) that stimulate fibroblasts to produce collagen nodules, progressively stiffening the lungs. OSHA tightened its permissible exposure limit for silica to 50 µg/m³ in 2016; the International Agency for Research on Cancer classified inhaled crystalline silica as a Group 1 carcinogen in 1996.
 Mars dust contains silicates and amorphous silica in its mineral inventory. Amorphous silica is generally considered less acutely toxic per particle than crystalline quartz, but the combination of silicate minerals, reactive iron, and perchlorates in a particle fine enough to reach the alveoli represents a multi-agent exposure without an established combined-effect model — a gap the NASA Martian Dust Limit Working Group explicitly flagged.
 The closest historical analog remains Apollo 17 astronaut Harrison Schmitt, who experienced runny eyes and persistent throat irritation following EVAs in which lunar dust contaminated his suit and habitat — the first documented case of planetary dust exposure symptoms in a human. Lunar dust is mechanically more dangerous than Mars dust because the Moon's lack of wind erosion leaves grains jagged and glassy; Martian dust grains are rounded by aeolian abrasion. But Mars adds what the Moon does not: perchlorate chemistry, reactive iron, and now, for the first time, confirmed ultrafine particles at the brain-transport threshold.
 NASA Sets Preliminary Exposure Limit Before Anyone Has Landed
 In February 2026, NASA convened a Martian Dust Limit Working Group to establish preliminary crew health standards before crewed missions arrive. Over two sessions on February 20 and February 27, the panel recommended a 24-hour time-weighted average exposure limit of 0.1 mg/m³ for Martian dust particles smaller than 10 µm, intended to govern missions of up to 30 days.
 The proposed limit is derived from NASA's existing lunar dust limit of 0.4 mg/m³ with a threefold uncertainty factor applied to account for Mars dust's additional chemical hazards — particularly perchlorate and reactive iron — whose long-term physiological effects at low doses remain incompletely characterized. The panel found NASA's approach "appropriately conservative for early short-stay missions" but recommended explicitly addressing short-duration spikes, particularly the post-EVA period when astronauts bring dust-laden suits back through the airlock.
 NASA is incorporating the limit into Volume 2 of NASA-STD-3001, the agency's human factors and environmental health standard for spaceflight. Separate spacecraft maximum allowable concentrations for specific Martian chemicals — including perchlorate and manganese — will serve as crosschecks alongside the particle-size limit.
 Shaunna Morrison, a Martian mineralogist at Rutgers University who contributed to the Working Group, described Mars dust as an unusual challenge due to its extreme fineness and its tendency to electrostatically cling to surfaces — a property that makes contamination-control approaches more difficult than on Earth.
 Engineering Solutions Being Developed Before Anyone Lands
 The research team and the NASA press release accompanying the study identify several engineering approaches being built into current mission planning.
 Suitports and dual-chamber airlocks are habitat architecture designs that prevent dust-covered suits from entering the pressurized crew environment. In a suitport configuration, an astronaut enters the suit from behind while it remains docked to the exterior of the habitat wall; the dust-covered outside of the suit never contacts the living space . Dual-chamber airlocks allow one chamber to be decontaminated before the inner door opens, limiting how much dust can migrate inward.
 Electrodynamic Dust Shields (EDS) use oscillating electric fields to repel charged dust particles from surfaces without mechanical contact. An EDS system was tested on Firefly Aerospace's Blue Ghost Mission 1 lunar lander in March 2025, demonstrating that electrically generated fields can actively clear dust from surface panels. Scaling EDS technology to spacesuit fabric or habitat viewport surfaces is an active area of NASA research.
 Material selection, now revealed by VanBommel's data to be a particle-size-sorting decision, adds an additional engineering lever that was not previously understood in this light. If suit designers know which polymer chemistries preferentially capture ultrafine versus fine particles, they can design the outer layer of suits to minimize concentration of the most medically dangerous size fraction — or use the differential adhesion as a filtering mechanism in a multi-layer suit architecture.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Is Mars dust dangerous to humans?
 Yes, in specific and compounding ways. Martian dust contains particles fine enough (≤2.5 µm) to penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream, plus ultrafine particles (≤100 nm) that can travel via the olfactory nerve directly to the brain — bypassing the blood-brain barrier. On top of the physical size hazard, Martian soil contains perchlorates at concentrations 100 to 1,000 times higher than typical Earth soil, which disrupt thyroid hormone production, plus reactive iron oxides that can generate free radicals in lung tissue. NASA's Martian Dust Limit Working Group proposed a preliminary safe-exposure limit of 0.1 mg/m³ for a 24-hour period but acknowledged the combined-chemistry risks remain incompletely understood.
 What chemicals are in Mars dust?
 Martian dust is a mineral mixture dominated by iron oxides (which give Mars its characteristic red color), silicates, and perchlorate salts. Perchlorates (ClO₄⁻) are present at roughly 0.5 to 1 percent by weight — confirmed at Phoenix, Curiosity, and now Perseverance landing sites — and block the thyroid gland's iodide-uptake mechanism by inhibiting the sodium-iodide symporter . Reactive nanophase iron oxide particles can generate oxygen free radicals on contact with lung tissue. Silicate minerals in the fine-particle range carry risk of silicosis-like lung fibrosis with long-duration exposure. A 2025 GeoHealth analysis also identified arsenic and beryllium in composition .
 Does spacesuit fabric choice affect which dust particles astronauts inhale?
 More than previously understood. VanBommel's study found that Teflon and Vectran — two materials already carried on Perseverance's SHERLOC spacesuit swatches — attract different particle size classes through electrostatic charging. Teflon preferentially accumulated ultrafine particles in the sub-100 nm range; Vectran concentrated particles at the larger end of the fine-particle spectrum, averaging around 2 µm. Because ultrafine particles are the size class most capable of traveling to the brain via the olfactory nerve, a Teflon-dominant suit outer layer concentrates the most neurologically hazardous fraction. Suit designers now have direct Martian surface data indicating that material selection is a particle-hazard-stratification decision, not merely a mechanical durability one.
 How will astronauts on Mars deal with dust?
 Three engineering strategies are currently being developed, and no single approach is sufficient on its own. Suitports and dual-chamber airlocks keep dust-covered suits from entering pressurized habitats; Electrodynamic Dust Shields, tested on the Firefly Blue Ghost lunar lander in March 2025, use oscillating electric fields to actively repel charged particles from surfaces; and material selection research, now informed by the VanBommel particle-size-sorting data, may allow suit outer layers to be designed to minimize accumulation of the most hazardous ultrafine fraction. The 2026 NASA Working Group recommended that crewed Mars mission architecture treat dust prevention as a layered engineering problem built into habitat and suit design from the outset, not retrofitted after first exposure data is gathered based on NASA Perseverance dust findings .
